PLAN: pick a target (any planet, the Moon or Pluto), write a mission statement, plan the orbit with live delta-v, trip time and next launch window, and split the budget into launch vehicle, spacecraft, science and reserve. The plan becomes the objectives.

FLY: a real-scale solar system with planets on JPL orbits for the real date, patched-conic gravity, atmospheres, re-entry heating, parachutes and landing legs. A burn planner on the map shows spheres of influence and transfer windows and plans transfers, corrections and captures. The planned orbit glows dark green. Science only counts once it is sent home.

Built in Lua with LOVE 2D; runs offline on ordinary laptops. Limitations: single player, 2D.
details:
PROJECT NAME

OrbitForge

HIGH-LEVEL PROJECT SUMMARY

OrbitForge is a space mission design game where players plan a complete mission and then actually fly it. Players pick a target (any planet, the Moon or Pluto), write a mission statement, plan the target orbit with live delta-v and launch-window estimates, and split a budget between launch vehicle, spacecraft, science and reserve. They then build a rocket from parts that each have mass, cost, power and data trade-offs, and fly it in a real-scale solar system built from NASA/JPL data, using transfer windows and planned burns for encounters and captures. At the end, a mission report explains why the mission succeeded or failed, so players learn how the engineering decisions connect.

LINK TO PROJECT DEMO

[paste the public Google Drive link to OrbitForge_demo.pdf]

LINK TO FINAL PROJECT

[paste the public Google Drive link to the folder with OrbitForge-windows.zip, orbitforge.love and the source code]

DETAILED PROJECT DESCRIPTION

What it does

1. Plan: a four-step mission planner. Choose the target body; write the mission statement; plan the orbit (periapsis, apoapsis, orientation), seeing the orbit drawn, its period and speeds, the delta-v needed for launch, transfer, capture, landing and return, the trip time and the next launch window; then split the budget into launch vehicle, spacecraft, science instruments and reserve, against suggested values. The plan becomes the mission's objectives.

2. Build: a drag-and-drop rocket builder with capsules, probe cores, tanks, engines (chemical, efficient vacuum, nuclear thermal, ion), decouplers, side boosters, fairings, heat shields, parachutes, landing legs, batteries, solar panels, RTGs, antennas, data recorders and six science instruments. Every part has a cost and mass; instruments draw power and produce data; antennas have data rates that fall with distance squared; solar power falls with distance from the Sun. The build screen shows the target, the delta-v the plan needs versus what the rocket has, and spending per budget category. You cannot launch over budget.

3. Fly: a real-scale solar system where the planets move on JPL orbits for the real date. Patched-conic gravity, atmospheres, drag, re-entry heating, parachutes, staging and landing. A burn planner on the map shows each body's sphere of influence, the next transfer window, and plans transfer burns, mid-course corrections and capture burns; the planned orbit glows dark green around the target. Science only counts once it is sent home by antenna or carried home in a recovered capsule.

4. Evaluate: a score (objectives, science returned, accuracy of the final orbit versus the plan, and money left over) and a mission report that explains causes, for example data stuck on board because the antenna is too weak at that distance, a probe out of radio range that cannot be commanded, a landing faster than the safe limit, or spending more than planned on a category. It compares plan versus actual for budget and orbit.

Benefits

It turns the abstract trade-offs of mission design (mass, power, data, communications, budget, orbit, time) into decisions with visible consequences, and players can replan and refly as many times as they like. It runs offline on ordinary laptops.

How it was built

Lua with the LOVE 2D game framework. Orbital mechanics use Kepler's equations (universal-variable propagation) for the planets and planned trajectories, and numerical integration for powered flight. Built and tested with automated headless tests.

Limitations

Single player only (team roles are planned for the future). The world is 2D, in the plane of the planets. Planets do not rotate.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

I’m a one-person team. I designed the game and directed all of it: what to build, how it should play, which real NASA data to use. I tested it throughout, found the bugs and decided every change. I used Claude (an AI assistant by Anthropic) as a programmer: it wrote most of the Lua code to my bugfixing reports and playstyle issues and helped draft the slides and this text. with its help i was able to recreate my vision. I sketched all of this out on paper beforehand and made it come into code with its help. I gave it the necessary prompts and it made and fixed the code to make it work.

NASA DATA

- NASA NSSDCA Planetary Fact Sheets (radius, GM, atmospheric density and scale height for each body): https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/planetfact.html

- NASA JPL Solar System Dynamics, Approximate Positions of the Planets (orbital elements and their rates, used to place the planets on the real date): https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/planets/approx_pos.html

- NASA JPL Planetary Satellite Mean Elements (the Moon's orbit): https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/sats/elem/sep.html

- NASA NSSDCA ring fact sheets for Saturn, Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune (ring radii): https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/satringfact.html

- Spacecraft hardware figures based on NASA missions: the ion engine uses NASA's NSTAR (Deep Space 1, Dawn) thrust and specific impulse; the RTG uses the MMRTG's mass and power.

SPACE AGENCY PARTNER DATA AND OTHER REFERENCES

- LOVE 2D game framework (https://love2d.org), zlib licence.

- push.lua screen-scaling library for LOVE.

- Sutton-Graves relation for re-entry heating; Laplace sphere-of-influence formula; Hohmann transfer equations.
